title: Archuleta County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: In Archuleta County the median well depth is 150 ft and the median yield is 10 gpm. Learn about local drilling costs, water levels, and buyer risks.
h1: Water wells in Archuleta County, Colorado
intro_html:
Archuleta County wells are classic mountain-bedrock wells. Most tap fractured rock, with a few in named formations like the Mancos and Dakota. Depth and yield can change fast over short distances, so the county-wide patterns matter when you price a new well or judge an existing one.

These numbers come from 3,769 permitted wells on record. They give a solid picture of how deep drillers are going, how much water they usually find, and what that means for cost and risk on a rural property here.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Archuleta County
sections.html:
Across Archuleta County, the median well depth is 150 feet. The middle half of wells land between about 65 and 260 feet, so most new domestic wells will be bid in that range, with contingencies to go deeper if needed. About 34% of wells are under 100 feet, while 44% fall between 100 and 300 feet.

Deeper drilling does happen: 16% of wells run 300–600 feet and 6% go past 600 feet. The 90th percentile depth is 450 feet, and the deepest well on record reaches 2,950 feet. Almost all wells are in an unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer, which is why there’s such a spread. Expect a driller to talk in terms of ranges, not a precise target depth.

sections.heading: What kind of well yield to expect here
sections.html:
For production, Archuleta County actually looks pretty favorable compared to a lot of mountain areas. The median reported pump yield is 10 gallons per minute, and the middle half of wells fall between 5 and 15 gpm. Over half of wells (54%) are in that 5–15 gpm band, which is plenty for a typical household on an exempt domestic permit.

High producers are not rare: 25% of wells test over 15 gpm. On the low side, about 18% come in between 1 and 5 gpm, which can still work with storage. True problem wells are the small group under 1 gpm, at 3%. That share is small, but it’s enough that you don’t skip checking nearby well logs before committing to a lot.

sections.heading: Water levels and what they say about the aquifer
sections.html:
Only a fraction of Archuleta County wells have a recorded static water level, but the ones that do show pretty workable conditions. The median depth to water is about 42 feet below ground, with the middle half of readings between roughly 10 and 100 feet. That means many wells have a decent water column without needing extreme total depth.

Looking at time, the median static level in the 2010s was 44 feet and in the 2020s it’s 41 feet. That’s a slight shift toward shallower water, not a drawdown trend. Keep in mind, these numbers are from individual wells in fractured rock, so local conditions can still vary a lot between properties and even along the same road.

sections.heading: Who has been drilling here and how activity has changed
sections.html:
Archuleta County’s drilling record goes back to the 1950s, but things picked up in the 1970s with 493 permits and stayed strong through the 1980s at 469. The 1990s were the busiest decade with 744 permits issued. Activity stayed high in the 2000s with 671 wells, then eased to 493 in the 2010s and 219 so far in the 2020s. The newest permit on record is from 2025, so new wells are still going in.

Most wells are domestic or household use (about 75%), with smaller shares for irrigation, stock, and monitoring. The main drillers showing up in the records are Beeman Bros Drilling Inc, Justice Water Systems, Inc, and Smith Water Well Service, each with a few hundred wells logged in the county.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost
sections.html:
Archuleta County sits on fractured granite and gneiss, which are slower to drill than soft formations. Typical drilling rates here run about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s median depth of 150 feet, the drilled hole alone pencils out around $9,800–$15,000.

Once you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a finished domestic well at that median depth usually ends up roughly $15,800–$27,000. If you hit one of the deeper scenarios around 300–450 feet, you scale those numbers up accordingly. That’s why it’s important to look at the full depth range in your specific area, not just the median.

sections.heading: Risks: low yield, dry holes, and water quality
sections.html:
With fractured-bedrock wells, the main practical risk is variable yield. Countywide, only about 3% of reported wells are under 1 gpm, but another 18% fall in the 1–5 gpm range, where you may rely more on storage and careful management. The presence of some very deep wells and a 450-foot 90th percentile depth tells you that a few properties needed more drilling to find adequate fractures.

On the quality side, mapped data within roughly 10 miles show 12 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 10 historic mine features, but no EPA Superfund cleanups. That doesn’t mean a problem on a given parcel, just that you should budget for a good lab test on any existing well, especially for a family home or if you’re near mining or industrial activity.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot in Archuleta County
sections.html:
Archuleta County’s numbers are encouraging: lots of domestic wells, a 10 gpm median yield, and many wells in the 100–300 foot range. But the fractured rock and the spread in both depth and production mean due diligence is critical on any single parcel, even if it’s not far from Pagosa Springs or Arboles.

If there’s already a well, pull the permit and verify reported depth, yield, and static level. If there’s no well yet, study nearby permits and have your driller quote a realistic depth range, not just the median. Factor in well and septic layout early in your site plan so setbacks and access don’t limit where you can build or put a driveway.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Archuleta County, Colorado?
faq.a: Based on 2,295 wells with reported depth, the median well in Archuleta County is about 150 feet deep. The middle half of wells are between roughly 65 and 260 feet. About 34% of wells are shallower than 100 feet, while 44% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Only about 6% extend past 600 feet, with a 90th percentile depth of 450 feet.

faq.q: What is a good well yield in Archuleta County?
faq.a: Archuleta County wells show a median pump yield of 10 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 5 and 15 gpm. Over half of wells fall in that 5–15 gpm range, which is generally plenty for a single-family domestic system. About 25% of wells exceed 15 gpm. Only around 3% are under 1 gpm, the range where daily use can become challenging without extra storage.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Archuleta County?
faq.a: In Archuleta County’s fractured mountain bedrock, typical drilling costs run about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s 150-foot median depth, the borehole alone usually runs around $9,800–$15,000. By the time you add casing, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, a finished domestic well at that depth is commonly in the $15,800–$27,000 range, with deeper wells costing more.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Archuleta County?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well. Regional data show 12 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 10 historic mine features within about 10 miles, but no EPA Superfund cleanups. Most wells tap fractured-bedrock aquifers, which can vary property by property. Before drinking the water from any existing well, plan on a full lab test for bacteria, major minerals, and any contaminants of local concern.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping in Archuleta County wells?
faq.a: The limited static water level records do not show a clear decline. The median depth to water in the 2010s was about 44 feet below ground surface, and in the 2020s it is about 41 feet. That suggests relatively stable, even slightly shallower, average water levels in the wells that were measured. Individual wells can still behave differently, especially in fractured rock, so local data are important.
